How to read this

This is the one place where everything we have learned about our build harness sits together. I wrote it so that anyone on the team, including people who were not in the working sessions this record comes from, can pick a piece of work, see why it matters and see what has already been tried. Throughout, “I” is me and “we” is the team.

Every number says how sure we are of it

MMeasuredCounted or timed on our own machine or in our own records.
EEstimatedWorked out from measured data with a stated assumption.
GGuessA judgement, written down so a measurement can replace it.
SSetting or outside figureA configured value, or a number from an outside study or vendor.
TTargetA bar we set for ourselves to clear.
IIllustrativeAn example that shows the arithmetic. It is not a result.

Every idea shows how far it has got

IdeaIdea. Proposed, or picked out of an outside source to try. Not yet designed.
DesignedDesigned. Written into a design or plan with its test, or chosen for adoption. Not built yet.
BuiltBuilt. It exists, but has not been measured or is not switched on yet.
TestedTested. Measured, trialled or replayed, with results in. The results may be strong, modest or a lesson.
In useIn use. Part of how we work today.
ParkedParked. We chose not to pursue it for now, or a better idea replaced it. It stays in the record with the reason, so nobody has to rediscover it.

Ids, terms and sources

  • The seven metrics are throughput, efficiency, token count, token cost, time taken, quality of output and hallucinations. Part 2 defines each, and every bottleneck and idea in this edition says which of them it moves. Bottlenecks in Part 2 are numbered 1 to 11; each groups the register’s rows that share one cause. Six ideas came only from my chats and were added on 14 November: PAR-22, TOK-44, MTH-66, MTH-67, MSR-49 and MSR-50.
  • Ideas are numbered by theme: MAC-03 is the third idea in the machine theme. The twelve theme codes are listed on the first page of Part 3.
  • Bottlenecks keep the ids given by the session that found them. B01 to B21 come from the bottleneck compile of 11 November. R2, R4 and B3-LOOP are loops of harness v2 (our 11 November design for the whole harness, set out in Part 1) that are bottlenecks in their own right. W1 to W5 (weaknesses) and L1 and L3 (two of its three levers, not the four token levers of Part 2) come from the Dex Horthy sweep, our card-by-card study of Dex Horthy’s talks and writing, which scored every outside idea against them. Ids that start with TK (tokens), LIB (the library, the knowledge store and the graph test, our held-out test of a typed code store), MC (the machine and the check) or PR (process; not a pull request) were added in this compile for bottlenecks that had no id yet.
  • Loops in the harness design are written as “loop R1” or “loop B2” in running text. Three loops are also bottlenecks with their own register ids: R2, R4 and B3-LOOP. R marks a loop that feeds itself, B a loop that pushes back toward a limit.
  • Terms. The first time a technical term appears it is explained in place. Every term is also in the glossary at the back, with a plain definition and where it comes from.
  • Sources. Every idea and number traces back to a document or to my session notes. The sources page says where each one lives, including the documents not yet committed to the repository, and the evidence folder holds the extraction with a citation for each record. The last page says how this compile was put together and checked.
One page

The short version

I build software with AI agents. The harness is everything around them: how I split work into sessions, the checks that decide whether work is right, and the memory that carries what we learn. I judge it by seven metrics: throughput, efficiency, token count, token cost, time taken, quality of output and hallucinations. This reference edition says what limits each one, what we have measured, and every idea we have against it, including the ones we only talked about.

97 % M
of our context tokens are the model re-reading a window it has already seen
574k–974k M
tokens in the orchestrator’s window each time it had to compact
2 of 2 M
compaction summaries we checked were wrong about the latest state
6,600 ms M
for one model step, against 0.5 ms M to read a file: time goes on steps, not on disk
1
The window keeps growing, and that is the first bottleneck. Every call re-reads the whole window, so each step costs more than the last, and the orchestrator’s window reached 574k to 974k tokens M before it compacted. Both summaries we checked were then wrong about the latest state M. My proposal is to run orchestration as a B+ tree spread over sessions, as in a distributed system: a session past about 40 % S of its window (set per model) splits, small ones merge, and we may never have to compact. WP12 wrote the rule and replayed it on our record: tokens are not settled against compacting earlier, and its first aim, fewer hallucinations, needs a live trial. I said yes to one trial wave at 300k, ahead of most of our compactions.
2
Hallucinations and quality have catches, not yet a rate. We recorded 20-plus overstated reports, with no denominator M, and those two wrong summaries M. 64 % M of reviews sent a slice back, and an Opus reviewer found a serious defect in 9 of 14 M Opus-built slices. Two things should bring the numbers down: claims that a script rechecks instead of a model, and windows that stay small (not yet measured). A script rechecked 1,265 M paths, commits and pull requests in FixFlow’s summaries: 16 M were not borne out, no more than in maintained documents; the latest state needs a reader. WP8 counts reports next.
3
One orchestrator and one usage limit cap throughput. Review, merging and checks all pass through one session, and when the five-hour limit hits, every lane stops: ten were stopped within about 15 minutes M. The testbed had about three lanes worth running M but ran six to nine M. The planner, the merge queue and the governor are designed to answer this.
4
Every agent pays a fixed start, often on the most expensive model. About 70k tokens M per clinic agent before any work, 27 % E of all our tokens. A short tool list should shrink it; model tiers by role are in use, and raising only the stuck problem to the top model is designed but not yet measured.
5
Most steps only find and re-read. 64 % M of FixFlow’s calls and 52 % M of the clinic’s only read or searched, each one a full re-read. A typed code store found more of what a change touched than a scripted search did (+0.076 overall M, the gain in the mobile app). The test with an agent in the loop is next.
6
What one session learns, the next does not have. The library and the knowledge store are designed, not built. The ensemble of simulated runs I suggested on 12 November helped: it showed which unknowns matter most. The same model’s corner settings (MEM-15) show the library pays only when work comes back, reaches the cheap model and is right, all together. Neither can pick a path, because the inputs are still guesses G.
7
A lot already works, and the work splits cleanly. The clinic’s full check is 3.0× faster in parallel M and 1.6× faster in a Linux container M. Sixteen packages each have a goal, a first deliverable and a “done when”: one has begun, six can start today, six start on my word and three follow another package.

What I need from you. Read this page and Part 4, take a package (two people can share one) and write your name on its card. Parts 2 and 3 are the reference for your package: the bottlenecks it answers and every idea we already have for it.

Part 1

What we are building

FixFlow is the product. The harness is how we build it. This part says what the harness is, where our ideas came from, and the design that ties them together.

What I mean by the harness

When I say harness I mean everything we wrap around the AI models to build software with them:

  • Sessions and agents. A session is one conversation with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which reads and edits code and runs commands on our PC. A session can start subagents (helpers that each begin with a fresh context) and workflows (scripts that run many subagents to a fixed plan).
  • Checks and gates. The test runs and reviews that decide whether a piece of work is good enough to merge into the main line of code.
  • Memory. Whatever carries what we learned from one session to the next: notes, the library we have designed, the knowledge store.
  • The token budget. A token is the unit a model reads and writes in, a short piece of text: a common word is often one token, a long word several. The context window is everything the model holds in mind for one call, and it re-reads the whole window on every call. Our Claude plan allows a limited amount of use in each five-hour window, so tokens are the resource every part of the harness shares.
  • The machine. The one PC everything runs on: its power, memory, disk and Docker (the tool that runs our databases and Linux test runs in containers).
  • How results reach me. Reports, visual pages and decision forms.

The word comes from software testing, where a test harness is the code that runs the tests. Teams that build with AI agents now use it for the whole system around a model.

Where the ideas came from

Two of our own projects feed this record:

  • FixFlow, the workshop management system we are building for a home-appliance repair shop in Karachi: a web app for the manager, an Android app for technicians and a backend in FastAPI (a Python web framework). Its build is laid out in the ship plan, the document that orders FixFlow’s work into phases (P0a, P0b and on).
  • The clinic testbed, an earlier large build on this same PC that we used to push the harness hard: 432 commits and 65 merges in eight working days M. Most of our measured bottlenecks come from its record.

Two outside sources were studied card by card: talks and writing by Dex Horthy of HumanLayer, author of “12-Factor Agents” and of “Advanced Context Engineering for Coding Agents”, and BAML, BoundaryML’s language for typed model calls. The glossary says more about each.

How it fits together: harness v2

On 11 November we put what we had learned into one design, harness v2. It treats the harness as one system with four scarce things: time on the check, review, the one-at-a-time merge, and tokens per five-hour window. Each scarce thing gets a part that controls it.

Speed = lanes × what one lane delivers, until the lowest limit. A lane is one session building one slice of work. More lanes help only until the first of the four limits is reached. Past that point, the knee, they add queues, tokens and collisions, and no speed.

The parts and what each one controls

PartIts jobControls
PlannerWorks out, before any work starts, which slices can run side by side and how many lanes are worth running.loop B5, lanes at the knee
SchedulerTurns the plan for a wave (a set of slices run together) into running sessions, and brings them back after a stop.loop R4, the pile-up
GovernorKeeps the five-hour usage window from stopping everything: it slows lanes before the limit does.loop B3, the limit stop; loop R2, context growth
LanesWhere the work is written. Each lane is a session that asks the library before it explores and leaves its results on disk.–
GateDecides whether a slice is good, by tests it runs itself.loop R1, the fix spiral; loop B1, check capacity
Merge queueThe one place where work is serial. It is a script, so the serial part is short.loop B2, the serial gate
LibraryThe harness’s memory. Written by the tools at the moment something becomes true. Sessions look things up in it when they need to, and it never pushes text into their context.loop R3, the library compounds; loop B4, staleness
MachinePower, restart, the off-machine copy and one always-on sensor logger. Everything above stands on it.–

The loops

The loop labels come from system dynamics, the method Jay Forrester began at MIT in the 1950s for studying systems as stocks, flows and feedback. A reinforcing loop (R) feeds itself: more of it makes more of it. A balancing loop (B) pushes back toward a limit.

LoopNameWhat happensWhat we saw in the testbed
R1The fix spiralA fix adds new stored state (a hold, lock, marker or cutoff), and one of the ways that state can end is never tested. That becomes a new defect, which needs another fix and another check.2.8 M review rounds per slice; 64 % M of reviews sent the slice back.
B1Check capacityEvery round needs the check, and the check can run only as many rounds at once as it has slots, each taking a full run time. Past that, lanes queue.One slot in practice (a second opened only with 8 GiB S free, which never happened) and 367 s M per run on Windows. Longest wait 2,030 s M.
B2The serial gateReview and merging pass through something that takes one at a time. Nothing leaves faster than that.The orchestrator briefed reviewers, read the last diff, ran the check twice and edited the wave board by hand.
B3The limit stopTokens rise with the lanes working and the context each carries. At the five-hour window’s limit every lane stops at once.14 M limit episodes in October; ten lanes run at once hit the limit within about 15 minutes M.
R2Context growthEvery call re-reads the whole context and adds to it, so each call costs more than the one before.Sessions on Sonnet ran to 963k tokens M; sessions on Opus compacted near 367k M.
R4The pile-upA waiting lane still holds its context. Waiting costs tokens, tokens bring the stop sooner, and after a stop everything restarts at once and waits again.All sessions were released together on 9 November; one check then waited 2,030 s M.
R3The library compoundsEach merged slice writes what it learned. The next session asks the library before it explores, so it reads less, finishes sooner and writes more.Not built yet. This is the loop we most want to start.
B4StalenessCode changes. An entry whose files changed is not trusted until its check runs again, so the library never fills with things that are no longer true.On the wave board, 183 M minor findings had no status.
B5Lanes at the kneeMore lanes help only until the lowest limit. Past it they add queues, tokens and collisions, and no speed.Lanes were chosen by feel and nothing checked for collisions; for the first two slices, the first check on merged main failed on hand edits to shared documents M.
Part 2

The bottlenecks

A bottleneck is whatever limits one of the seven metrics I judge this work by. Most of them limit any team that builds with AI agents; the troubles of our own PC come last. This part gives where we stand on each metric and each bottleneck with what we measured, then how we found them, the token and machine measurements, and the full register.

The seven metrics, and where we stand

Which bottleneck limits which metric

Agents sorted every bottleneck in the register and every idea by the metric it moves and by its cause. The causes group into the eleven bottlenecks below.

The bottlenecks, one by one

Each block names the metrics the bottleneck limits (the two it limits most are filled in), says what happens, what we measured and what we have not, then lists ideas against it with how far each has got. Blocks 1 to 10 hold for any team building with AI agents; block 11 is our own PC and plan.

1The window keeps growing until it must compact or clear

LimitsToken countHallucinationsToken costQuality8 register rows · 30 ideas

What happens. Every call re-reads the whole window and adds to it, so our orchestrator and long-lived sessions accumulate tokens until they must compact or clear. The summary that then replaces the history can misstate the latest state.

What we measured. Cache reads are 96.8 % M of 7.35 B M context tokens, output 0.75 % M. The root compacted at 574k, 974k, 967k and 970k tokens M, though a second count of the same transcripts finds three compactions M. 2 of 2 summaries were wrong on the latest state M; the verbatim tail corrected both. Vendor figures, not reproduced here, put native compaction at 48.7 against 69.3 for the full history S (TOK-41). Our snapshot-and-restore trial matched native compaction on recall and task success but used 17.0 % more tokens M (TOK-12). Not yet measured. At what window fill a session’s judgement starts to fall, for any model, and whether a brief written at a split is right more often than a compaction summary.

Ideas against bottleneck 1, and how far each has got
PAR-22DesignedOrchestration as a distributed B+ tree: split and merge. Designed: my idea of 14 November, aimed first at hallucinations. Rule written and replayed on our record (below), not tested live. I said yes to a 300k trial; old summaries are read first.
TOK-44DesignedTake finished material out of a live window. Designed: asked for on 26 October, now settled inside the split rule. A new session starts from a brief that points at the repository, so finished material never enters it. Untested.
TOK-16BuiltCompaction snapshot, restore and recall hooks. Built: in the clinic testbed, not yet run live. 85 offline tests M, 53 defects fixed M. Restore quality not yet measured.
TOK-02In useEarlier auto-compact window of 400,000 tokens. In use for Opus: 84 of the 117 M compactions in session windows are Opus, 81 M of them at 366–385k. Sonnet ran to 963k M and is not set yet.

2Agent reports claim more than was actually done

LimitsHallucinationsQualityEfficiencyToken cost15 register rows · 78 ideas

What happens. Agents report tests, evidence or runs that did not happen or do not match, and a model re-reading its own claims does not catch it. A check can also go green while testing nothing.

What we measured. 20-plus recorded overstatements, with no denominator M. 5 of 6 high-risk final commits went unread M. A citation check re-located 109 M claims, none dead, and 575 of 579 M quotes matched exactly. Not yet measured. What share of claims are false: overstatements are counted without a denominator yet.

Ideas against bottleneck 2, and how far each has got
REV-38DesignedSkeptic verdict rules with an unverifiable outcome. Designed: confirmed needs a traced path, refuted needs counter-evidence, otherwise unverifiable with what would settle it. Not yet tested.
REV-11In useCitation check over every claim. In use: 109 M claims re-located, none dead; 575 of 579 M quotes matched exactly. It checks existence only.
CHK-04In useTest-id accounting and planted-fault demos. In use: in the testbed, six planted faults gave CHECK FAILED M, and no test id ran twice. Not yet in FixFlow CI.
REV-30DesignedClaims file checked by a script each round. Designed: a script reruns each cited test at parent and head. Not yet run. Replay first, false flags under 10 % T.

3One orchestrator reviews and merges everything, and its window overflows

LimitsThroughputTime takenToken countEfficiency11 register rows · 33 ideas

What happens. One root session reviews, merges, edits the board and reads every agent’s report, so work leaves only as fast as it does. Its window keeps growing until it must compact, and one usage limit stops every lane together.

What we measured. Root compacted at 574k, 974k, 967k and 970k tokens M (a second count of the same transcripts finds three compactions M), about 499k per call M, 15.3 % of November tokens M. Subagents made 91 of 104 limit errors M. Ten lanes were stopped by the limit within about 15 minutes M. Not yet measured. Whether a gate workflow stops root compaction, and how cache reads count against the limit.

Ideas against bottleneck 3, and how far each has got
PAR-10In useBounded session tree: depth three, fan-out three. In use: my proposal of 2 November; 12 slices and about 20 follow-up branches merged in 8 days M. The root still became a serial gate; PAR-22 is its next form.
PAR-13DesignedPlanner that sizes lanes just below the knee. Designed: plan accepted 11 Nov, nothing installed. The testbed had about three lanes worth running M but ran six to nine M.
PAR-02In useLane sessions: one phase, own worktree, run together. In use: eight lane sessions started on 13 November M and PRs #187–#192 opened that day M. RAM, not CPU, sets the ceiling M.
REV-28DesignedReview as a gate workflow with typed verdict. Designed: gain is bounded, the root is 15.3 % M of tokens. Target: no root compaction across five gates T.

4Each agent pays a fixed start and may inherit the top model

LimitsToken countToken costEfficiency8 register rows · 30 ideas

What happens. Every agent window first loads system prompt, tool and connector schemas, skills, memory, CLAUDE.md and its brief, then re-reads it every call. Fan-out multiplies it, and an unpinned agent inherits the session’s model, even for a simple lookup.

What we measured. About 70k M tokens per clinic agent before any work (about 60k E per FixFlow agent): tools 34k, connectors 17k, skills 9k, system 8k, memory 2k M. That fixed start is 27 % E of all our tokens and 47 % E of FixFlow’s. Not yet measured. What tiering and a stripped prefix actually save: no per-tier spend is recorded yet.

Ideas against bottleneck 4, and how far each has got
MTH-39DesignedEscalation ladder: raise only the stuck problem a tier. Designed: on guessed inputs, 25.7 G cheap-call equivalents, 21.2 % G wrong, versus 29.9 G and 11.2 % G strong model alone.
MTH-66IdeaFast mode for a fleet of subagents. Proposed: fast mode was on for a 132 M agent run on 3 November. Effect on time and tokens not measured yet.
TOK-23DesignedStrip the fixed prefix with a short tool list. Designed: tool definitions are 34k M of the 70,000 M each agent pays. Pass bar: 20 runs T, zero refused writes.
MTH-08In useModel tiers by role, raise effort before tier. In use: 12 M agent definitions pin Haiku, Sonnet or Opus. Tiering has no cost measurement yet.

5Agents spend most calls just finding and re-reading things

LimitsToken countEfficiencyTime taken8 register rows · 35 ideas

What happens. Over half our calls only read or search, and each call re-reads the whole window. Fetched file content stays and is re-processed every later call, and a small set of files recurs across sessions.

What we measured. FixFlow: 64 % M of calls, 55 % M of tokens only read or search. Fetched content fills 26 % E of windows; 72 paths M hold half. One model step takes 6,600 ms M, a 93 KB file read 0.5 ms M. Not yet measured. Whether any graph, map or recall aid makes an agent finish faster: 0 M agent runs.

Ideas against bottleneck 5, and how far each has got
MSR-50TestedTime model steps against disk reads. Tested: a model step takes 6,600 ms M; a file read 0.5 ms (possibly a warm read), a 618-file search 124 ms M. Count steps saved.
RET-06TestedTyped symbol-level graph of the repo. Tested: recall 0.700 M vs 0.625 M for scripted search; the gain is on mobile (+0.151 M). No agent run yet.
RET-18BuiltTyped-edge map of the planning documents. Built: clinic testbed prototype, 3,361 records for 167 KB M; extraction recall 0.52 M. No agent has used it yet.
TOK-25IdeaBatch lookups into one command. Proposed: batching two lookups would remove about a third of all calls E and a third of their re-reads E.

6Each session starts without what earlier sessions learned

LimitsEfficiencyQualityToken costHallucinations21 register rows · 31 ideas

What happens. A new session knows only what the repo and memory files carry. Past diagnoses sit in prose nobody can search by symptom, so a recurring defect is solved again at the top tier, and docs drift from code.

What we measured. One missing-tool error was re-hit in 54 of 78 M sessions across 9 M projects. 3 to 5 M same-cause repeats among 48 M fix commits. 517 of 1,268 backticked file names in docs do not resolve M. A cold-resume trial recovered 10 of 10 frozen facts M. Not yet measured. How often similar problems recur in our work, which decides whether a library pays.

Ideas against bottleneck 6, and how far each has got
MEM-13BuiltEnsemble of simulated runs over the pathway map. Built: my suggestion in the library-pathways chat of 12 November. 1000 S runs per setting; 51 M of 60 M unknowns are guesses. It helped by ranking what to measure first. On those guesses the library was cheaper and no more wrong than the escalation ladder in only 0.3 % G of runs, or 6.1 % G when its unknowns move together, and the model shows it pays only when much work comes back, reach is high and entries are good (cost 0.82 G, wrong 0.67 G; MEM-15). It cannot pick a path on guessed inputs. A trained tree ensemble (MEM-68) is not started.
MEM-56IdeaMerge partial solutions through a graph. Proposed: not yet tested. In real walks two checked answers did not make a checked merge (6 cases M); tests will decide.
MEM-21DesignedKnowledge store of solved problems. Designed: nothing built. Same-cause repeats are 3 to 5 M among 48 M fix commits; the recurrence audit decides whether to build.
MEM-02In useMemory file holds pointers, not restated state. In use: memory now points to where state lives; the rewrite found and corrected one M stale next step.

7Fixes create new defects and gaps surface late

LimitsQualityTime takenThroughputEfficiency12 register rows · 36 ideas

What happens. A fix can add new stored state whose endings no test covers, so each fix round makes fresh defects and the rounds do not converge; ours did. Work tested only on synthetic data lets first-use gaps surface on the last day.

What we measured. Round one found 19 high-severity (P1) defects M, and the fixes made at least 5 more P1 and 10 P2 M. 64 % of reviews sent a slice back, 2.8 rounds per slice M. Two M first-use gaps surfaced on the final day. Not yet measured. How many fix-made defects a two-round fix contract would prevent; its replay has not run yet.

Ideas against bottleneck 7, and how far each has got
REV-01In useTwo-level merge gates with refute-reviewers. In use: every testbed slice; 9 of 11 M gates took three rounds, and fixes created at least 5 M more P1.
REV-22TestedFresh critics check each plan revision’s changes. Tested: the v6-to-v8 delta check found 1 blocker, 20 major, 20 minor M before work started; findings folded into the next version.

8Lanes queue behind one slow check slot

LimitsTime takenThroughputQuality8 register rows · 18 ideas

What happens. Every lane must pass the full check before merging, and checks share limited machine capacity, so lanes wait in line. On our PC, Windows also adds a slow hop to the database.

What we measured. 19 recorded waits: median 409 s, longest 2,030 s M. Parallel workers cut a full run from 855.2 s M to a mean of 283.8 s M, about 3.0×. Two slots gave 1.8–1.9× throughput M. Linux container check: 230.1 s M against 367.2 s M on Windows. Not yet measured. One check’s peak memory, so we cannot yet size slots safely.

Ideas against bottleneck 8, and how far each has got
CHK-01In useParallel check with one database per worker. In use: 855.2 s M became a mean of 283.8 s M, about 3.0× faster. Eight workers gain only 3 % M.
CHK-26BuiltLinux container check, proposed as the gate. Built: mean 230.1 s M against 367.2 s M native, about 1.6× faster, and found 2 failures M Windows missed.
CHK-22TestedTwo container checks at once. Tested: 266 s and 267 s M together against about 440 s M in a row, least free memory 5.3 GB M.

LimitsEfficiencyQualityHallucinationsToken cost17 register rows · 71 ideas

What happens. We learn of a false statement only when a reviewer, a script or I catch it, and no context aid has run with an agent in the loop. So we cannot yet tell whether a change helps.

What we measured. 20-plus recorded overstatements, with no denominator M; 2 of 2 compaction summaries wrong on the latest state M. A script rechecked 1,265 M paths, commits and pull requests in FixFlow’s 61 M recorded summaries: 16 were not borne out, 1.3 % M, no more than in two maintained documents. 0 M agent runs with a context aid. November token tally: 4,252.9M M cache-read tokens; re-measurement agreed within 0.3 % M. Not yet measured. Whether a fuller orchestrator window degrades its judgements; keeping context under about 40 % S is an outside rule of thumb.

LimitsThroughputTime takenEfficiency17 register rows · 44 ideas · specific to our PC and plan

What happens. Everything runs on one PC that powers off without warning and is short of memory. After a stop, Docker, databases and sessions wait for me to restart them, and merges and starts wait for my approval.

What we measured. About three days idle after the 6 Nov power-off M. 25 shutdowns since 1 October M, 15 with no Claude call ten minutes before M. After a 28-minute M outage all eight M lanes resumed from their worktrees. Dropping Docker’s cache gave back 2.2 GB M. Not yet measured. What causes the power-offs, and who holds memory when it runs short.

The bottleneck compile of 11 November sorted each of its bottlenecks into one of four classes, and the register (our joined list of every bottleneck, later in this part) keeps them: Build (we know the fix and it needs building), Decide (it waits on a decision from me), Diagnose (we need one measurement to find the cause) and Trial (we try a fix and measure it).

Where the tokens go

We counted every model call on this PC for both projects: 35,834 calls M and 7.35 billion context tokens M. The finding is simple and useful. Token use is calls × window size. 97 % M of all tokens are the model re-reading a window it has already seen; what it writes is 0.75 % M. So the way to spend fewer tokens is fewer calls and smaller windows, not shorter answers.

The two projects show the same mechanism in two shapes. The clinic testbed ran one big window: its main sessions held 74 % M of its tokens at about 333k tokens per call. FixFlow ran many small windows: 1,118 agent windows M of about 12 calls each, and 56 % E of the tokens inside each agent window was its fixed start (47 % E across all of FixFlow’s calls, main session included), about 60k tokens E, most of it the descriptions of tools and connectors (plug-ins that link Claude to outside services).

Checked and ruled out. These looked like suspects and are not: the model mix (routing changes the price per token, not the count), file reads (re-reading a file inside the same window is only 0.5–1.5 % M), any one file (the busiest is 1.5 % M of its project’s tokens) and my prompts (231 M real prompts across both projects, about 155 E calls for each). The usage is in the agents’ own automated steps, which is good news: steps are what we control.

Still to learn. How re-read tokens count against the plan’s five-hour limit is unknown to us. Until we know, we treat a cut in tokens as a saving in usage and measure separately whether it also means fewer stops.

The machine and the check

The clinic testbed ran 432 commits and 65 merges in eight working days on one PC M. Its record shows where the time went and, better, where we have already won a lot of it back.

24 M
unexpected shutdowns of the PC, 7 October to 10 November
2.8 M
review rounds per slice; 64 % M of reviews sent work back
2,030 s M
longest wait for the one check slot
~70k M
tokens every clinic testbed agent re-read before doing any work

The first three numbers set the agenda for the first three phases of harness v2; the fourth, the ~70k every agent re-reads, is work for the token budget (phase 5, WP5). The machine comes first because everything stands on it: of the 25 power-offs M logged from 1 October to 11 November (a longer window than the 24 above), 15 M came with no Claude call in any project in the ten minutes before, so the cause is still to be found. The protections are known and cheap: no sleep on mains power, an always-on sensor logger, a resume list that brings sessions back two at a time and a verified copy of the work off the PC. Working from separate worktrees already pays: when the power went for 28 minutes on 13 November, eight FixFlow lanes were cut off mid-turn and all of them resumed from their worktrees M. The check comes second because that is where the measured wins already are, and the review rounds come third, as scripts that cost no tokens.

Part 3

The ideas

Every harness idea we have had, whatever its results so far: 484 M ideas in 12 themes. Each one says the problem it is meant to solve, how it works, where it stands and what comes next. Ideas that were tried and taught us something, or that we parked, stay in the list with what we learned, so nobody has to rediscover them.

All ideas at a glance

CodeThemeThe kind of problem it coversIdeas
MACKeep the machine up and the work safeThe one PC: power-offs, restarts, resuming after a stop, off-machine copies, memory, Docker and disk, and keeping secrets out of agents’ reach.35
CHKFast, fair, trustworthy checksThe test run that decides whether work is right: speed, the Linux container gate, check slots, fair queues, heartbeats, clean-up, and checks that can really fail.43
REVReview and fix rounds that convergeReviewing work and fixing what review finds: fix rounds, claims checks, fresh reviewers, refuters, severity, reading the final commit, and merging.60

MAC
Theme · 35 ideas

Keep the machine up and the work safe

12 in use · 1 tested · 1 built · 14 designed · 4 ideas · 3 parked   Work packages: WP1WP2a

Everything we build runs on one PC. Between 7 October and 10 November it powered off unexpectedly 24 times M. Of the 25 power-offs since 1 October, 15 M came with no Claude call in any project in the ten minutes before, so our own load alone does not explain them. The clinic testbed still lives only on this machine.

The ideas here keep work safe when the PC stops and bring it back without me: an off-machine copy, a resume list that brings sessions back two at a time, and an always-on sensor logger that will show why it powers off. Separate worktrees already pay: when the power went for 28 minutes on 13 November, all eight FixFlow lanes resumed from their own copies M. This theme is harness v2 phase 1, and I answered its first six decisions on 11 November; a full restart chain waits, because I chose to keep Docker’s start at sign-in off for now (D03).

CHK
Theme · 43 ideas

Fast, fair, trustworthy checks

21 in use · 4 tested · 2 built · 8 designed · 4 ideas · 4 parked   Work packages: WP2aWP2bWP3

The check is where our biggest measured wins already are. Running tests in parallel took the clinic check from 855.2 s to 283.8 s M, tracing start-up took a 16-test run from 43 s to 11.5 s M, and the Linux container run takes 230.1 s against 367.2 s natively M.

What remains is making it the one gate everyone trusts: sized from measured memory, fair in its queue, visible while it runs, and never green when it tested nothing. FixFlow’s gate harness already carries several of these ideas into daily use; harness v2 phase 2 does the rest.

IdIdea and how it worksThe problem it solvesWhere it standsNext step

Eight workers gain only 3% M.Keep as the speed baseline; re-measure the worker count for FixFlow's backend, which needs per-worker databases.

REV
Theme · 60 ideas

Review and fix rounds that converge

21 in use · 1 tested · 4 built · 17 designed · 12 ideas · 5 parked   Work packages: WP3WP7WP9WP10a

In the clinic testbed a slice took 2.8 review rounds on average M, and 64 % of reviews sent the slice back M. Some fixes created new defects, some reports claimed more than was done, and in 5 of 6 high-risk merges nobody had read the final commit M.

The ideas here make review converge and make its verdicts checkable: a contract for each fix round, scripts that test claims, fresh reviewers that try to refute, and a merge queue that records who read what. Harness v2 phase 3 turns the strongest of them into six scripts that spend no tokens.

PAR
Theme · 22 ideas

Planning parallel work

10 in use · 0 tested · 0 built · 12 designed · 0 ideas · 0 parked   Work packages: WP3WP4WP12

More lanes help only until the first limit is reached, the knee. Past it they add queues, tokens and collisions. In the testbed, ten lanes run at once hit the usage limit within about 15 minutes M, while two at a time got further.

The ideas here decide before a wave starts which slices can run side by side, how many lanes are worth it and where they would collide. Since 13 November FixFlow’s ship plan runs a coordinator session with one lane session per phase, so this theme is moving from design into daily use.

TOK
Theme · 44 ideas

Spend fewer tokens per result

7 in use · 6 tested · 4 built · 8 designed · 11 ideas · 8 parked   Work packages: WP5WP6aWP12

We counted every model call on this PC for both projects: 35,834 calls and 7.35 billion context tokens M. 97 % of those tokens were re-reads of a window the model had already read M, so the number of calls times the size of the window is what we have to manage.

The ideas here are the four levers the token report found, the governor and the written budget of harness v2, and smaller habits that keep windows short. Each lever is sized as an exposure, the share of tokens it could touch, which tells us where to aim; the savings themselves are what the next measurements will show.

MEM
Theme · 71 ideas

Remember what we learned

5 in use · 3 tested · 8 built · 35 designed · 17 ideas · 3 parked   Work packages: WP6aWP6bWP6cWP7WP8

Every new session starts without what the last one learned, unless something carries it across. The ideas here give the harness a memory: the knowledge store designed in PR #183, the reasoning-cache library of harness v2, and smaller habits such as turning a lesson into a check.

My goal for the library is that a cheaper model finishes more of our work at the same quality. The pathway map shows, step by step, where an entry can be lost before it helps, which tells us what to build first. Both designs are complete on paper and unproven so far; their first steps are cheap tests built to prove them.

Theme · 30 ideas

Find the right code fast

5 in use · 11 tested · 5 built · 3 designed · 5 ideas · 1 parked   Work packages: WP7WP8WP10a

Before an agent can change code it has to find what the change touches. On 75 held-out FixFlow commits, a typed store of code facts put 0.700 of the touched files and definitions in front of the reader within an 8,000-token answer M, ahead of a scripted search at 0.625 M. The gain sits in the mobile app; outside it the two are still too close to call.

The three engines we tried, one relational and two graph, gave identical answers, so the engine can be chosen on speed, size and effort. The test was a fixed script with no agent in it. Next comes a zero-token index replay; the wider test I asked for, with an agent in the loop, knowledge graphs, time and caching, follows under a written budget once I settle GT-1.

Theme · 67 ideas

How we orchestrate

17 in use · 1 tested · 3 built · 20 designed · 17 ideas · 9 parked   Work packages: WP3WP4WP6bWP10a

Our method is written down in the orchestration design of 31 October: a main session that plans and judges, cheaper models that discover with citations, and fresh-context reviewers that try to refute what was found. This document was made that way.

The ideas here are how we brief agents, shape workflows, choose a model for each job and recover when an agent fails or returns nothing. Many are in use every day; the rest are refinements we have designed and can now test.

We want one source for each.B13 · B04In useIn use in the clinic build, and it became a bottleneck itself: board state 221 KB M, root edits caused failing checks at two slices, and docs were stale at wrap-up.Replace with slice-written fragments and a generated board; add a test that fails when lock-step edits diverge.

SKL
Theme · 27 ideas

Skills, agents and tools

1 in use · 0 tested · 17 built · 2 designed · 5 ideas · 2 parked   Work packages: WP5WP6bWP9WP10aWP10b

A skill package teaches agents one domain; a project agent is a saved agent definition with its own model, tools and instructions. PR #185 holds 13 skill packages and 11 project agents for FixFlow.

The ideas here cover what to package, how to keep each agent’s fixed start small, how to know a skill is used, and which outside tools are worth borrowing.

MSR
Theme · 50 ideas

Measure, model and test ideas fairly

6 in use · 10 tested · 2 built · 15 designed · 12 ideas · 5 parked   Work packages: WP2aWP3WP5WP6aWP6bWP7WP8

Every number in this document carries a tag that says how sure we are of it. That habit, and most of the measurements in it, came from this theme.

The ideas here are how we measure and how we keep a test fair to the idea it tests: tallies from our own transcripts, replays on recorded work, held-out test sets frozen before the run, models of the whole system, and rules such as testing the strongest form of an idea against the strongest baseline.

IdIdea and how it worksThe problem it solvesWhere it standsNext step

Two container checks run together took 266-267 s M each, against 220 s M for one run alone in the same test.Run the sampler on the Windows PC itself to diagnose shutdowns and idle-session memory.

Part 4

Dividing the work

This part turns the record into work. Sixteen packages between them carry every bottleneck in the register and every idea in Part 3. Each card says what the package is for, where it works, its first deliverable, how we will know it is done and what it waits on. Six can start today, one has begun (WP12), six start the day I give my word, and three follow another package. Before you take one, read the box under the map: it holds the few rules that keep two people, two projects and one PC from getting in each other’s way.

How the packages fit together

Before you start

Two projects, one PC. Each card says whether it works in FixFlow (this repository) or in the clinic testbed. Work on a branch, never on main. The ship plan and this compile live on the plan branch (PR #182), the knowledge-store design on PR #183’s branch and the skills on PR #185’s branch.

The ship plan comes first. Before you use the Docker gate or start an agent, look at the lane board in docs/program/W0-results.md on the plan branch. If a FixFlow phase is running or waiting on its reviewer, harness work that needs the gate or agents waits.

One budget for the whole team. The two-lane cap and the written token budget (D07) are shared by all of us, not per person. Any Claude session that draws on my plan counts as one of the two lanes, your own working session included. Book agent runs in the shared queue and launch nothing on your own; WP11 sets the queue up first, and until it exists a run waits for my yes. The cap is for harness work; FixFlow’s lanes follow the ship plan’s own rule.

One limit on heavy checks. Both projects share this PC’s 31 GB M of memory, so a heavy check from either project takes a slot from FixFlow’s machine-wide lock, ff-slot.sh, like any FixFlow job. That lock is the one shared limit. Leave its pools and slot counts as they are; WP2b may propose how waiters are ordered, not how many run.

The coordinator writes FixFlow’s program files. A package that would change the ship plan, the lane board or FixFlow’s gate scripts sends a proposal to the coordinator. The coordinator brings it to me, and once I say go, the coordinator writes it.

Machine traps that already cost us time. Never prune Docker networks or restart Docker: other sessions run containers. Anything that needs its own Docker network gets an explicit subnet inside 10.77.0.0/16. With MSYS_NO_PATHCONV set (the Git Bash setting that stops it rewriting paths), write paths as C:/…. Clone into scratch folders with git’s core.longpaths setting on (git -c core.longpaths=true), because Windows otherwise refuses long file paths. There is no python on PATH; our scripts run with Node. Never touch the antivirus.

The work packages

Each card says what the package is for, which bottlenecks and ideas it carries, the first thing to deliver, how we will know it is done, and the kind of person it suits. Each size carries its tag: E where a design estimated it, G where it is my guess until the first step reports; a package not yet sized says so. Write your name on the line when you take one.

WP1Machine and recovery

Owner
No power-off costs us work or a day. The work is copied off the PC every night, sessions come back from a resume list, and an always-on sensor logger records power, temperature and memory, so the next power-off can be diagnosed. This is harness v2 phase 1.
Moves most: throughput and quality
Works in: This PC and the clinic testbed repository; scripts and settings only, on a branch.
Bottlenecks it answers
13 in the register: B05, B10, B11, MC-FS, MC-DOCKERCACHE, MC-AV, MC-TOOLS, MC-PREBUILD, MC-INJECT, MC-CPU, MC-HOOKCOST, PR-SECRETS, B03.
Ideas it carries
25 ideas: 8 in use, 1 tested, 1 built, 11 designed, 2 at the idea stage, 2 parked. Part 3 tags each one WP1.
First deliverable
Today: the bundle-and-verify script and the nightly copy script. They must also capture the six M folders in the clinic repository that are in no commit (register row B11) and the untracked harness documents. After I plug in and encrypt the drive, which comes after FixFlow’s P0a: the first verified copy.
Done when
A clone from the copy shows the same heads, and the copy is never more than 24 hours old T. After one real reboot, done in a quiet window with my go, the resume list appears at sign-in with “start Docker” as its first line, and once Docker is up the databases in use are healthy within 3 minutes T with no further command. The next unexpected shutdown leaves a logger trace that ends at it.
Good fit for
Windows administration, PowerShell or bash scripting, git.
Size and dependencies
One to two days of one session E, scripts and settings only, no agents. Needs nothing from another package. Mechanisms 7 and 8 (one fact, one command; a session parks itself when its record and branch disagree) come in here, because they cost one line in a brief.
Waiting on me: Switch off sleep on mains power (D04); plug in the drive and switch on its encryption (D02); install the sensor logger and debugger (D05); write down the days the house lost power; say yes to the nightly copy as a scheduled task and to permission rules that deny agents the Railway commands railway up (deploys to the live host) and railway run (runs a command with the live settings); later, D08 (a battery backup) once the diagnosis is in. My steps come after FixFlow’s P0a.

Median gate near 230 s T, zero Linux-only failures on main, no gap between heartbeats longer than 60 s T, the next stall names its test, and after each merge the worktree and container counts return to the active slices plus one.

Docker and Linux, test runners (pytest, Vitest, Jest), queues.

Bottlenecks it answers
2 in the register: PR-P0A, PR-OWNERWAIT.
Ideas it carries
23 ideas: 9 in use, 3 built, 7 designed, 3 at the idea stage, 1 parked. Part 3 tags each one WP11.
First deliverable
One decision board that joins harness D01 to D23, the knowledge store’s KS-D decisions, the graph-test decisions and links to the FixFlow items of mine that the harness touches (kept in docs/program/W0-results.md, not copied), each with a distinct prefix and what it unblocks; beside it, the shared queue where agent runs are booked.
Done when
No package waits more than a day T on a decision of mine, with each wait logged.
Good fit for
Front-end and data visualisation, clear writing.
Size and dependencies
About a day for the board G. Needs nothing; every package feeds it.
Waiting on me: Answering the board. “Accept all defaults” covers only decisions that stay on this PC and spend no money; installs, hooks, permissions, scheduled tasks, deletes, a rented host and anything that leaves this PC each keep their own yes.

WP12Orchestration B+ tree: split and merge on context

Owner
Stop any session, the orchestrator first, from growing until it must compact or clear: run orchestration as a B+ tree in the manner of a distributed system, where a session that passes a set share of its window splits by scope and small siblings merge.
Moves most: token count and hallucinations
Works in: Transcripts on this PC, read only, for the replay; later one trial lane wave in a FixFlow or testbed worktree.
Bottlenecks it answers
1 in the register: TK-FILL.
Ideas it carries
2 ideas: 2 designed. Part 3 tags each one WP12.
First deliverable
Done on 14 November: the split rule and a replay over 97 M recorded session windows at no token cost, both checked twice (docs/program/SPLIT-RULE-2026-11.md); then a fill gauge, a trial measure and a scripted hand-over check. That script found 16 of 1,265 M paths, commits and pull requests in the 61 M FixFlow summaries on record not borne out, 1.3 % M, no more than in two maintained documents, so the trial is scored by a reader’s check of the latest state. Next: that check on a sample of those summaries, the baseline.
Done when
One trial lane wave runs under the rule with no compaction, and its hallucination catches (wrong hand-over claims first), rework and tokens per result are set beside a matched wave that compacts earlier at the same token count.
Good fit for
Data structures and distributed systems (B+ trees, range splitting), transcript analysis (JSON), Claude Code sessions.
Size and dependencies
The rule and the replay took a day. The trial needs ten or more hand-overs per arm G; the baseline says whether that is enough. The baseline and the trial start agents, so both wait on D07; the trial acts on the same tokens as lever 1 in WP5.
Waiting on me: I said yes on 14 November to one trial wave at 300k, the only one of the three lines replayed that comes before our Opus compactions. Still mine: D07 before any agent run; which lane wave is which arm; the Opus compaction setting of 400,000 S raised to 433k E or above if an Opus session holds a node under the rule; and opening each new root.

How we work

These are the rules we follow or are adopting now, collected so a new person can work the same way from day one. Each says where it comes from.

RuleWhat it means in practiceFrom
Seven metrics first, and chats countEvery bottleneck and idea names the metric it moves (throughput, efficiency, token count, token cost, time taken, quality of output, hallucinations) and the number we have for it; where there is no number yet, we say so. An idea said only in chat is recorded with its session and line.My correction of 14 November
The ship plan comes firstFixFlow’s next phase is never delayed or edited for harness work. Harness work takes neither the Docker gate nor agent lanes while a FixFlow phase is running or waiting on its reviewer: the gate shares this PC’s memory and slots, and the agents share the same usage limit.Harness v2, standing rules
One budgetLanes two at a time. A token budget written down before any launch. One change that adds agents per five-hour window. Stop starting agents after the first empty result, which can signal a usage limit.Harness v2, §6
Script before agentModels find things; scripts decide whether a finding is closed. A check a script can make is never left to a model.Harness v2, standing rules
Replay before liveA gate or review mechanism is accepted by a replay on our own record wherever one is possible, and runs record-only before it may refuse anything.Harness v2, standing rules
One fact, one commandA fact about this PC or the tools becomes a rule only after one command has checked it. Our first list carried five facts that turned out wrong.Harness v2, mechanism 7
My yes for anything that reaches outsideNo hooks, installs, scheduled tasks, permission changes, deletes, rented hosts or anything leaving this PC without my decision.Harness v2, standing rules
Discover without judging, and cite everythingDiscovery agents extract what the sources say, each claim with a citation in the form path:line — quote. Ranking and verdicts come later, from someone else.Orchestration design
A fresh pair of eyes before a decisionAnything that becomes a decision is checked by a fresh-context skeptic told to refute it, booked like any other agent run; D07 itself, a zero-token proposal that comes before any agent budget, gets my own review. Verdicts are confirmed, partly confirmed, refuted or unverifiable, and an unverifiable one names what would settle it.Orchestration design, verification policy
The right model for the stepThe orchestrating session plans and judges; Sonnet discovers and maps; Opus deep-dives and verifies; Haiku looks things up. A step gets the cheapest model that passes.Orchestration design, tier guide
Tag every numberMeasured, estimated, guess, setting, target or illustrative. A computed number takes the weakest tag of its inputs.Bottleneck compile and library pathways
Test the best form of an ideaResearch and build the strongest version, compare like with like, define the scoring before the run, and fix anything that would handicap one arm instead of noting it as a limitation.My feedback to the sessions
Answer the question that was askedTest the architecture as I described it, with the popular tool itself as one arm. A clean answer to a narrower question is not the answer.My feedback to the sessions
State lives on disk, in the repoPlans, results and decisions are files, so a stopped session can resume and anyone can pick up a package.Orchestration design; harness v2
Glossary

Every term, and where it comes from

399 terms, grouped by where they come from and sorted A to Z inside each group. “Coined by us” means the term was made up in one of our own documents, named after it.

Our own terms

Addendum 2026-11-09 A second pass that added 36 M sources and 311 M cards (X posts, SlopCodeBench article, Tessl episode, local transcriptions) without re-clustering the families.Coined by us in section 4 of the Horthy document, 2026-11-09.
Alone and last weights Alone: the effect of moving only one limitation's unknowns. Last: what is lost if only that one stays unsolved. Both are shares of the full fall (see Full fall).Coined by us in model-brief.md R19, 2026-11.
Analyst The Opus agent that reads the live repository in a deep-dive lane and returns ranked, evidenced findings. Analysts produce claims; skeptics check them.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.
Architect / lens One of four M Opus agents, each reviewing the architecture from one viewpoint such as offline sync or Android platform.Coined by us for the harness review panel.
B01 to B21 Ids of the 21 M open bottlenecks of the testbed build, listed on 2026-11-11 (for example B01 fix rounds, B04 serial orchestrator). Distinct from loop ids B1 to B5.Coined by us in evidence/harness-bottlenecks/bottlenecks.md.
BAML item ids (B-, D-, I-, P-, R-, S-, T-) Ids of the 89 M BAML idea cards by source lane: B blog, D docs, I independent evidence, P prior art, R repo, T talks; S-1 to S-5 are structural borrows.Coined by us in the BAML sweep, PR #184.
Binding review / merge-ready The review the coordinator dispatches to a fresh Opus agent on the PR head SHA. A PR is merge-ready when gates and CI are green, the verdict names the head SHA, nothing holds it, and the coordinator read it.Coined by us in SHIP-PLAN sections 7.1 and 7.7.
Bottleneck compile (11 November) Our map of the 21 M clinic bottlenecks B01 to B21, each with a class, a first step and a proof, and of how the outside ideas fit them, in docs/program/HARNESS-BOTTLENECKS-2026-11.md. Not to be confused with this compile (this document), which joins everything.Coined by us, 11 November 2026.
Bottleneck family One of the nine groups the register sorts its bottlenecks into, such as Machine, Check, Review or Memory. Part 2 lists them, and the heat map in Part 3 counts the ideas aimed at each.Coined by us in this compile.
Brief The written instruction given to a session or subagent.Ordinary usage; the clinic orchestration page.
Build-ahead / entry line / stack / at risk / merge-hold list Build-ahead: starting a phase before its entry condition is met when the unmet item is not code it needs. Stack: build on a reviewed branch tip. At risk: a PR label. Merge-hold list: PRs held as draft.Coined by us in SHIP-PLAN-2026-11.md section 7.2.
Card ids (A#-##, CR-##) Ids of mechanism cards extracted from testbed records: A is the sweep (A5 context system, A6 corpus map), CR the root's compaction and context lessons. There are 158 M cards.Coined by us in sweep-cards.txt.
Cheap model / strong model The low-cost tier (Sonnet, or Haiku for lookups) used for routine reading and checking, against the high-cost tiers (Opus and Fable) kept for judgement. The escalation ladder moves work up, from the cheap model to Opus to Fable, only when needed.Library design (LIBRARY-PATHWAYS); the cheap-call equivalent is measured against this pair.
Cheap-call equivalent The library model's cost unit: one call by the cheap model (Sonnet) costs 1 I; other costs are multiples of it.Coined by us in library-pathways model-brief.md, 2026-11.
Check (the seven steps) / container mode The clinic's full check: ruff, format, mypy, Django’s own checks (the clinic is a Django web app), migrations, database probe, pytest. Container mode runs it in a Linux Docker container: 230 s M versus 367 s M on Windows.Clinic scripts/check.py and linux-test-runner task.
Check slot (check lock, Docker-gate slot) A machine-wide permit to run the clinic’s full check, so heavy checks wait their turn instead of colliding on this PC. The clinic set up two S slots but opened the second only when 8 GiB S of memory was free, which never happened, so in practice it had one, with waits up to 2,030 s M. FixFlow’s equivalent is a slot of ff-slot.sh (see ff-gates.sh / ff-slot.sh / slot).Coined by us in the testbed faster-check task.
Circuit breaker A script rule that stops issuing agents when fresh null results suggest a usage limit, halting with HALT and not_started lists.A general software engineering pattern, applied in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN section 4.3.
Citation check A Sonnet pass that confirms quoted text exists where claimed and has not moved or been fixed.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.
Claims file A file each slice commits listing what it claims, so a script can check every cited test exists, ran, and fails when its guard is removed.Bottleneck B12; over 20 recorded overstatements M motivate it.
Class: Build, Decide, Diagnose, Trial Bottleneck classes. Build: the remedy is known. Decide: my choice. Diagnose: a measurement will find the cause. Trial: plausible but not yet measured.Coined by us in the bottleneck compile (11 November 2026).
Clinic testbed My earlier large clinic-management build on this PC, used to exercise and measure the harness. Its record is the source of the 21 M bottlenecks and most measured numbers.My earlier project; evidence summarised in docs/program/evidence/harness-bottlenecks/.
Codex adapter The testbed's tool that snapshots and restores working state around compaction. It was built for Codex and evaluated three times.Built in the clinic testbed for OpenAI Codex.
Cold-resume trial / cold resume A test where a fresh agent must recover ten S frozen facts from the repository and PR alone, to show a phase can be resumed.Coined by us in the ship plan (P1 trial).
Context system (snapshot/restore, read admission, recall, resident input) The clinic's tool around compaction. Snapshot saves declared task state and restores it verbatim; read admission limits big file reads (over 30 KB S); recall searches transcripts by words; resident input is what sits in the window.Coined by us in the clinic's tools/context_system.
Context tokens processed The tokens the model read, summed over every call, including cache reads.Measure defined in TOKEN-BOTTLENECK-2026-11.md.
Coordinator session In the ship plan's parallel execution, the single session on the plan branch that owns the plan, shared results, contracts and the merge call, and never writes feature code.Coined by us in SHIP-PLAN-2026-11, section 7.1.
Corners / all-good setting / tie Corners set each condition group at its poor or good end. All-good puts every library unknown at its good end. Tie is how strongly a group's unknowns move together (0 independent, 1 shared).Coined by us in model-brief.md revisions 4 and R18b, 2026-11.
Corpus map (cmap), status model S1-S6, query levels L1-L3, frontier, dangling endpoint A versioned map of the clinic's planning documents, with edges and line spans, built by cmap.py. Statuses: attested, codebook, overlay, reconstructed, candidate, derived. Frontier: unexpanded referents. Dangling endpoint: named but unspecified target.Coined by us in the clinic corpus-map design.
Coverage ceilings / oracle-match trial Coverage ceilings: long-run limits on what the library could hold for exact, similar or composite problems, drawn from outside studies. Oracle-match trial: give Sonnet the known-best earlier solution (the oracle) on past problems it has not seen, and score it by tests.Coined by us in model-brief.md and the 2026-11-12 library review.
CureFound My senior design project at GIKI (the Ghulam Ishaq Khan Institute, a university in Pakistan): rare-disease drug repurposing with routed specialist models, Neo4j and a checked language model. Harness research was mapped onto it.My own project; mapping in RESEARCH-RESULTS-FOR-CUREFOUND-2026-11-13.md.
D01-D23 (v2 decisions) Owner decision cards on the harness v2 page, each with a phase and a when-needed date.Coined by us in the harness v2 design.
Dead-citation statuses Citation-check outcomes: DEAD_CITATION (the cited line is gone), ALREADY_FIXED, and MOVED (the line drifted).Coined by us in the W2 workflow.
Delta check A critic pass that reads only what changed between plan versions.Coined by us in the harness review.
Design steps 1-10 / case families The ten steps: task arrives, trigger, query, match, delivery, use, check, failure and ladder, capture, afterlife. Ten case families group real cases; ids like f10-1b name family and case.Coined by us in the library design walks, 2026-11.
Device lab (L3) / lab accounts / edge 404 stand-in A native emulator rig with scripted protocols to rehearse the drain and offline matrix before a real phone. Lab accounts and keys are test-only. Stand-in modes mimic the unreachable host: edge404, 5xx or a hang.Coined by us in SHIP-PLAN section 7.5 and L3a, 2026-11.
Diff-restricted check (one-hop) A check limited to items a change touched, plus the files one import away.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.
Direct fit and supporting fit Direct: the idea would move the number the bottleneck compile gives as that bottleneck’s proof. Supporting: it makes a step of the first move cheaper, safer or checkable.Coined by us in the bottleneck compile, section 9.2.
Disposition: adopt, trial, already-done, skip The ruling on an idea family: adopt as is, trial with a measured test first, already done by the harness, or skip for weak evidence or low value.Coined by us in the Horthy and BAML sweeps.
E1 probes The planned adherence experiment: 10 T direct probes, which ask about a CLAUDE.md rule outright, plus oblique probes (which test a rule without naming it), all scored with a frozen rubric to see whether agents obey CLAUDE.md under different layouts or models. Planned, not yet run.Coined by us in the knowledge-store design (PR #183).
E1-E5 (library expectations) My five expectations: E1 big token cut over time; E2 faster responses and builds; E3 Sonnet at low effort matching Opus; E4 reuse across projects; E5 accurate, efficient lookups.Mine, stated on 12 November 2026.
Entry kinds (do_not_apply, open_defect, trap, unverified_seed, pending_anchor) A forbidden change, an unfixed defect, a gotcha, an entry awaiting its executable check, and an entry whose fix sits on a branch, in that order.Coined by us in the knowledge-store design, 2026-11.
Entry, handle, footprint (knowledge store) Entry: one stored lesson. Handle: a key it is found by (error template, symbol, paraphrase). Footprint: the files, settings and versions it depends on, used to notice staleness.Coined by us; footprint adapted from build-system dependency tracking.
Episode / piece of work One point where a result is produced and checked, about ten G cheap calls, visible or latent. A wrong output that passes the gate is an escape.Coined by us in library-pathways model-brief.md, 2026-11.
Escalation ladder The order a failed problem climbs: one cheap retry, then Opus, then Fable, with the solution stored on the way back.Coined by me in the library goal, 2026-11.
Evidence-status vocabulary Labels REPORTED, OBSERVED, DOCUMENTED, INFERRED, PROPOSED, UNKNOWN and VERIFIED that state how a fact is known.Coined by us in the clinic AGENTS.md.
ex1..ex8 worked examples Eight real past defects reconstructed from git history as first entries and test cases: ex6 correct-PIN lock, ex3 payment duplicate, ex4 dispatcher cursor, ex7 and ex8 Expo build traps.Coined by us in knowledge-store research lane R-02, 2026-11.
Exposure How much of the tokens sit where an idea or lever could act, for example calls past 200k. It is neither a saving nor a ceiling.Coined by us in the bottleneck compile and token report.
F01-F10 (effectiveness review) The ten numbered findings of the clinic testbed’s effectiveness review. They proposed four separate measures (quality, context, productivity, cost), a context freshness test, a frozen baseline and a throwaway deployment with backup and restore.Clinic testbed effectiveness review.
Failing condition The input or state under which a defect claim can be observed.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.
Fan-out and depth Fan-out is the number of children per parent; depth is the number of session levels below the root (here root, slice sessions, at most one child level).General usage; the clinic orchestration page.
ff-gates.sh / ff-slot.sh / slot ff-gates.sh runs backend, mobile or web checks in containers with a per-lane database. ff-slot.sh is the machine-wide lock. Since 13 November it has two pools: a light pool of 3 S slots for backend gate stacks, and a heavy pool of 2 S for Jest, Vitest, an emulator or a Gradle build, which takes its whole pool.Coined by us in phase L1.
Final head The last commit on a branch at the moment it merges. We want a reader to have read exactly this commit, not an earlier one.Bottleneck B17: 5 of 6 high-risk merges had an unread final head M.
Finding One concrete defect or gap a reviewer or scan reports, with a path:line citation and a severity. It closes only on a test the harness runs.Review practice in the ship plan and testbed; tracked in the finding table.
Finding board / finding table The record listing every review finding with severity and status. Testbed rows were prose thousands of characters long, so a table is proposed.Testbed practice; proposed as mechanism 4 in the bottleneck compile.
Finding id scheme (O01-F20, O3-F2) Analyst number plus finding number; O01-F20 is analyst O-01's finding 20.Coined by us at gate G2.
Finding ids (G05-01, GC-01, GS-15, FC-01 ...) Numbered clinic review findings. Letters name the slice or review family (GS, GT, GU, GV; faster-check FC and FS).Coined by us on the clinic task.md board.
Findings register / register id The table of verified findings with ids, severity and status (139 M findings at gate G2). A register id names a known defect a reviewer must confirm fixed, with a fail-before and pass-after test.Coined by us at gate G2 and in the ship plan.
Fix round / fix-round contract A pass that fixes findings. The contract: a test per finding that fails before and passes after, full gate before the fix commit, revert instead of patching, a fresh reviewer.Bottleneck B01 mechanism 9; to be replayed on recorded chains before live use.
Fixed prefix (fixed cost per agent) The roughly 70,000 tokens M each agent re-reads before doing work: system prompt, tool and connector schemas (34k M), skills, CLAUDE.md.Claude Code subagent behaviour; measured in card CR-11.
fixflow-explorer and fixflow-pr-reviewer Two project agents we built: a Haiku code locator, and a pull-request reviewer bound to a head commit that returns a verdict schema.Built by us in this repository.
Floor A cheap baseline (same directory, plain co-change, or scripted search) that any graph method must beat to count as a gain.Coined by us in the graph test protocol addendum 2, 2026-11.
Footprint (slice) The list of files a slice declares it will write. The plan check uses it to avoid collisions between lanes. Not the same as a knowledge-store entry’s footprint.Coined by us in the harness v2 plan check.
Fresh context A reviewer or agent started without the author's earlier conversation, so it cannot inherit the author's assumptions. Costs a new fixed prefix each time.Refuter and fresh-reviewer practice; about 70k fixed tokens per agent M.
Frozen validation contract A test sealed before any map or store is built: 5 S cases, 3 arms (a map, routed reading and Graphify), 2 S runs each and blind scoring; an arm counts as better only with a gap of 0.10 S in 4 of 5 cases. It keeps a pilot from being judged by rules chosen after the results.Our library and graph-test work (idea MSR-18), kept by WP8.
Full fall In the library pathway model, how far the library route’s cost and wrong rate fall, on average, when every library unknown moves from its middle value to its good end: 30.6 % G. Step and limitation weights are shares of it.Coined by us in model-brief.md (library pathway map), 2026-11.
Funnel A chart starting with 100 I pieces of work the cheap model would get wrong alone, showing how many remain wrong after each step toward a right answer.Coined by us when building the pathway page, 2026-11.
G0-G8 (measurement gates) The nine checkpoints, G0 to G8, of the clinic testbed’s planned measurement system (see M00-M06). They are not the G1 and G2 gates of the orchestration design.Clinic testbed measurement design (A7-09 to A7-12).
G1, G2 (gate records) Written records the main session made after W1 (G1) and W2 (G2): hypothesis verdicts, the verified defect register and decisions, before the next workflow was dispatched.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.
Gate A check a change must pass before merging: tests, lint, claim checks, and reviewers finding no open critical defect. Also the step that runs a store entry's own check.General software practice; our gate workflow is described in HARNESS-BOTTLENECKS section 3.4.
Gate script A plain JavaScript workflow script that gathers agent results and sorts them into buckets for the Fable judge.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.
Graph test Our held-out test of whether a typed code store (see that entry) finds what a change will touch better than search and simpler baselines, on commits the test had never seen. The typed store gained +0.076 M recall overall, with the gain in the mobile app.docs/program/GRAPH-TEST-RESULT-2026-11.md, 12 to 13 November 2026.
graphtest:1 The Linux Docker image, 1.26 GB M, in which every graph-test arm runs so the arms share one environment.Coined by us in the graph test engines-linux recipe, 2026-11.
H1-H5 (graph-test hypotheses) Hypotheses declared before scoring: H1 and H2 engines equal; H1b community prior; H3 typed graph against baselines; H4 questions; H5 engine speed and size.Coined by us in graph2 protocol addendum 3, 2026-11.
Harness The system we use to build software with AI agents: sessions, subagents, workflows, scripts, gates, memory, token management, the PC they run on, and how results reach me.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10; not the FixFlow product.
Harness v2 Our 11 November design for the whole harness: eight parts (planner, scheduler, governor, lanes, gate, merge queue, library and machine), the feedback loops between them, five phases, eleven mechanisms and decisions D01 to D23. Part 1 sets it out.docs/program/HARNESS-V2-DESIGN-2026-11.md, 11 November 2026.
Heartbeat / stall watchdog / stall limit A heartbeat is a periodic signal naming what a long check is doing. A stall watchdog kills a silent check; the stall limit is 600 s S. The check writes waiting, running or stalled.General systems practice; the limit is a testbed setting.
Horthy-sweep terms: card, family, blind reader, Reviewers A and B Card: one extracted idea with quote and claim (1,906 M). Family: cards with the same claim (838 M, then 861 M). Blind reader: a Sonnet that read without knowing our harness. Reviewers A (benefit-seeker) and B (cost-and-novelty skeptic) scored each family.Coined by us in the Horthy sweep (PR #186).
Hot set The small group of files, about 72 E paths, that holds half of the fetched tokens across sessions.Coined by us in the caching findings.
HR (harness review) / HR-... rulings HARNESS-REVIEW-2026-11-01.md and its labelled rulings (HR-A1a, HR-C1, HR-C4 and so on), binding on the plan from v6. HR-C4 is the 500k S context trigger that needs a sensor.Coined by us in docs/program/HARNESS-REVIEW-2026-11-01.md.
Hyper-V staging rig / Drills a-o A local Debian virtual machine sized like the proposed server, running fifteen M re-runnable drills: deploy, upgrade, backup, restore, load and security probe.Microsoft Hyper-V; the rig and drills are from the clinic staging-rig task.
Index replay A zero-token test: build an import-and-caller index at each recorded window's start, count the lookup-only calls it would have answered. First candidate trial of phase 3.Harness v2 design, phase 3 and decision D23.
Journal and index (knowledge store) The journal is an append-only folder of immutable event files in git, the source of truth. The index is a disposable SQLite database rebuilt from it for fast lookups.Event-sourcing pattern; chosen as proposal D in the knowledge-store design.
Judgement-free discovery Stage-1 agents return facts only, never comparisons, severities or verdicts. Judgement is left to the main session.Coined by us in ORCHESTRATION-DESIGN-2026-10.
Key table In the split rule, a repository file with one row per piece of work: owner, state and where its result is. A fresh inner session can take over from it.The split rule (WP12).
Knowledge store (ks) A planned local database and command-line tool where agents record solved hard problems, traps and failed approaches and later look them up by symptom. Designed in PR #183, not built or proven.Coined by us in KNOWLEDGE-STORE-DESIGN-2026-11.md, 2026-11.
KS-0..KS-9, KS-6b, KS-T The knowledge store's planned build phases, one session each: audit, journal core, retrieval, gate, seed, pilot, Docker gates, wire-in, second host, checkpoint. KS-6b is the executable gate; KS-T is teardown.Coined by us in the knowledge-store design, 2026-11.
KS-D1 to KS-D22 (knowledge-store decisions) My numbered decisions in the knowledge-store design, each with a default: KS-D1 run the recurrence audit, KS-D1b the build go-ahead, KS-D16 the embedding trigger, KS-D17 the CI caller-pin test, KS-D22 guarded_refs. The design writes them D1 to D22; this compile adds KS- so they never mix with the harness decisions D01 to D23.Coined by us in the knowledge-store design, 2026-11.
KS-R/A/C/F/K/O/P/V id series Id prefixes in the design: rulings (R), adjudication (A), refuted claims (C), refuter amendments (F), critic amendments (K), my critique O1..O20, refuter pass P1..P27, second-pass claims (V).Coined by us in sections 12.1-12.8 of the knowledge-store design, 2026-11.
L1-L3 (levers) Three levers ideas were scored against: L1 effort routing, L2 context budget and compaction, L3 output backpressure and verifiers. Not the ship-plan L1-L4 phases.Coined by us in HARNESS-IDEAS-HORTHY-2026-11.md.
Lane (session) One Claude Code session working one slice or phase in its own git worktree, in parallel with others, ending in a draft pull request.Coined by us in the harness v2 design and ship plan section 7.1.
Lead / candidate / miss; abstention Lookup outcomes: a lead is a confident, gate-checked match; a candidate is a weaker one; a miss is nothing found. Abstention means answering nothing when unsure.Coined by us in the knowledge-store design, 2026-11.
Lever A change that could cut token use, ranked by size in the token report.Coined by us in TOKEN-BOTTLENECK-2026-11.md.
LIM-01 to LIM-69 Ids of the 69 M limitations found by walking real cases through the library design's ten steps: 54 M seen in real cases, 15 M from thought experiments.Coined by us in limitations.json, 2026-11.
Limit episode One time the five-hour usage limit stopped agent work. October had 14 M.Our harness review and token measurement.
Load drill A test with many simulated users against the app: the 12-user drill M to be rerun on current main, then a bulk generator to 250,000 T stock movements.Bottleneck B20; harness v2 phase 4.
Look-alike (distractor) A misleading stored entry that matches a problem's symptoms but has a different cause.Coined by us in the pathway model, 2026-11.
Lookup A query of the knowledge store or library before exploring, triggered by an error, an escalation or a diff. It returns leads or abstains.Knowledge-store design; lookup-only calls are what the index replay measures.
M00-M06 / WF-01..WF-04 M00-M06 is the clinic's skipped measurement pipeline of recurring evals. WF-01..WF-04 are its workflow research stages: pilot, trial, measurement research, expansion.Clinic testbed documents.
Mapper and adjudicator Mapper: an agent that places each idea against the bottlenecks. Adjudicator: an agent that rules on flagged items; an item it does not restore stays out of the mapping.Roles in the bottleneck compile’s section 9 workflows.
Maturity scale The six labels we give every idea. Idea: written down, not yet designed. Designed: a written design exists. Built: the mechanism exists but has not been measured. Tested: measured or tried at least once. In use: part of how we work now. Parked: set aside for now, ruled out or replaced, and kept with the reason. A label is the furthest stage any source reports, which stops a design being described as a result.This compile’s own honesty rule: a label never claims more than its sources report.
Mechanisms 1 to 11 The eleven M artefacts the fitting ideas reduce to: 1 sealed replay, 2 verdict script, 3 transcript audit, 4 one finding table, 5 dry run with stand-in agents, 6 merge queue, 7 one fact, one command (facts backed by a command), 8 resume check, 9 fix-round clauses, 10 I read marked lines on high-risk merges, 11 a short tool list per agent.Coined by us in the bottleneck compile, section 9.3.
Merge queue A script that merges slices one at a time under a lock, runs the check on the merged result and applies the board diff. Designed in harness v2.Coined by us in the bottleneck compile, section 3.4.
Model step One call to the model inside a session: it re-reads the whole window, then acts once. The median step in November’s clinic sessions took 6,600 ms M.Our token measurement and the timing of 11 November (MSR-50).
Narrowed / over the cap Narrowed: the refuter let only a smaller version of the idea survive, and tables list that form. Over the cap: a family that reached no refuter because the per-group limit was hit.Coined by us in the Horthy sweep.
Notes file (task.md, wave board) A short repository file of state, decisions, ruled-out items and next action that a session reads to resume. The clinic task.md also held the status table and gate sections.Convention in the FixFlow and clinic harnesses.
Number tags M, E, G, S, T, I Evidence tags on every number: M measured, E estimated, G guess, S a setting or outside study or price list, T target, I illustrative. A computed number takes the weakest input tag.Coined by us in the harness documents.
